summary: A 1974 survey of how far different sites had gotten in implementing the new Telnet protocol on their servers. It is a status snapshot, not a specification. It updates RFC 702 and is itself updated by RFC 679.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher checks which students have finished a homework. This note checks which computers had finished building the new chat-by-keyboard tool.

questions: how many hosts had new telnet in 1974
subtitle: The November 1974 progress check on new-protocol Telnet servers across the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET community needed to know how many server hosts had actually switched to the new Telnet protocol.
tldr.mechanism: D. W. Dodds re-ran a survey from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on 4 December 1974 and listed what changed since the last report, plus an updated summary and table.
tldr.outcome: 16 of 37 server hosts (43%) had a new-protocol implementation. The author calls progress a snail's pace. It updates RFC 702 and is updated by RFC 679.

today: RFC 669 is a snapshot from late 1974. It updates RFC 702 and was updated by RFC 679, the February 1975 survey. The RFC index lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Last Survey
sections.content: Two months after the last survey, the author says new-protocol servers had appeared at the usual snail's pace. The list of changes (host numbers in octal) includes: SRI-AI (102) now has a new-protocol server; USC-ISI (126) and USC-ISIB (226) now have them; SDC-LAB (10) is back; SDC-CC (110) and HAWAII-500 (344) are coming on the net with status unknown; LONDON (52) was added; SDAC-44 (32) was removed; and BBN-TENEXD is now host 162.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists which computers joined, left or finished the new tool since the last check.

sections.title: The Summary Counts
sections.content:
The summary updates the one in RFC 702. Of 37 server hosts, 19 (51%) had no new-protocol server, 2 (6%) were of unknown status and 16 (43%) had a new-protocol implementation. Of those 16, 9 used the new protocol on socket 27 with the old one on socket 1, 6 used it on both socket 1 and socket 27, and 1 used it on socket 1 only.

The data come from a survey program plus a few manual checks, as seen from BBNA on 4 December 1974.
sections.plainLanguage: Out of 37 computers, 16 had the new tool, 19 did not, and 2 were a mystery.

sections.title: The Tabulation and Options
sections.content:
The table lists each server by host number and name, with entries for socket 1 and socket 27 (Old, New, X for no server, ? for not ascertained) and the options implemented. I# means the option is implemented incoming to the user (server says WILL #) and O# outgoing from the user (server says DO #).

Options implemented by anyone are 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark. The servers marked with an asterisk return improper responses to some Telnet option requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a checklist with a row per computer and columns for which new features it can do.

references.text: Dodds, D. W., September 1974 survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers, RFC 702.
